Latin similis like, simulare imitate and simul together belong to an attested historical family. Simultaneous refers to events at the same time, not specifically imitation. Preserve existing sim relation as historical lookup and distinguish actual Latin word/stem and sense.

English adjective thick is an independent base with documented compounds and verbs such as thicken and thick-skinned.
thick + skinned, literal skin thickness and a figurative sense of insensitivity to criticism.
thick + skulled, figurative dullness; not a claim about a literal skull measurement.
thick + -en, to become or make thick.
past/participle of thicken, from thick + -en.
agent/substance that thickens, derived from thicken + -er.
Thick + -en to make/become thick + -ing.
Thick + headed; figurative slow-witted sense is a semantic development, not literal anatomy in every use.
Thick + adverb-forming -ly.
Thick + -ness.
Thick + set; stocky or set/growing close together.

germ + -cide. English germ developed from bud/sprout through seed of disease to microorganism. Germicide kills microbes, not plant sprouts; the connection to the source root is historical semantic development.
